lede: Some data is too big or too slow to handle one row at a time on one computer. Apache Spark splits the work into pieces and runs them side by side, and PySpark lets you drive it from Python.
objectives: Explain what Spark does: process data in parallel, one partition at a time per core
Describe PySpark as Python's way to use Spark, and a DataFrame as a table Spark manages
Print rows with `show()` and count them with `count()`
Read a DataFrame's column names with `columns` and its types with `printSchema()`

blocks.md:
**Apache Spark** is an engine for processing data in parallel. It splits a table into **partitions**, chunks of rows, and works on several of them at the same time, one per processor core. On a cluster, many machines each take some of the partitions, so a job that would take hours on one computer can finish in minutes.

In this course Spark runs in **local mode**: one machine with 2 cores, so it works on up to two partitions at once. There's no cluster here, but the code you write is the same code that runs on one.

**PySpark** is Spark's Python API. You write ordinary Python, and Spark does the heavy work behind it.

The main thing you work with is a **DataFrame**: a table that Spark manages, with named columns, a type for each column, and rows. The `learners` and `courses` tables above are already loaded as DataFrames called `learners` and `courses`. To see what's in one, call `show()`.

blocks.title: Print a DataFrame's rows
blocks.note: `show()` prints the rows as a table, with the column names on top. There are five learners, each with five columns.

blocks.md: `show()` prints up to 20 rows. `show(n)` prints only the first `n`, and says so underneath. It also cuts any text longer than 20 characters and ends it with `...`. That's only for printing: the data itself is unchanged.

blocks.title: Fewer rows, and long text
blocks.note: With `show(2)` Spark prints two learners and adds `only showing top 2 rows`. In `courses`, the fourth title is longer than 20 characters, so `show()` prints it as `Data Modelling Ba...`.

blocks.md: `count()` counts the rows and gives back a plain Python number, so you can print it, mix it with text or do arithmetic with it.

blocks.title: Count the rows
blocks.note: Five learners and four courses. The header line that `show()` prints isn't a row, so it isn't counted.

blocks.md: Every DataFrame knows its columns and their types, together called its **schema**. `df.columns` is a Python list of the column names. It isn't a method, so there are no parentheses. `df.printSchema()` prints each column's name and type, and whether it may hold missing values (`nullable`).

blocks.title: Column names and the schema
blocks.note: `columns` is a plain list, so `len` counts the six columns. `printSchema()` shows that `lesson_count` holds whole numbers (`integer`) and `published_date` holds dates; `nullable = true` means a value may be missing.

blocks.title: Calling columns like a method
blocks.note: `columns` is already a list, so the `()` tries to call a list. Write `learners.columns`. `show()`, `count()` and `printSchema()` are methods, so they do need their parentheses.

blocks.md: The opposite mistake doesn't raise an error. `print(learners.count)` without parentheses doesn't count anything: it prints a description of the `count` method instead of `5`. If you see `<bound method ...>`, add the `()`.

concept.prompt: How does Spark make a big job faster?
choices: It splits the data into partitions and works on several of them at the same time
It reads the data one row at a time, very quickly
It keeps a copy of the whole table on every core
It skips the rows it doesn't need to print
concept.why: Spark splits a table into partitions and processes them in parallel, one per core. A cluster adds more machines, so more partitions run at once.

concept.prompt: In this course, where does Spark run your code?
choices: On a cluster of many machines
In local mode, on one machine with 2 cores
On a single core, one row at a time
concept.why: This environment runs Spark in local mode with 2 cores, so it can work on two partitions at once. There's no cluster, but the code is the same.

concept.prompt: What does `print(courses.count())` print for the `courses` table above?
choices: The four rows, as a table
concept.why: `count()` counts rows and gives back a plain number. The header isn't a row, and the columns are `len(courses.columns)`.

review: Spark processes data in parallel: it splits a table into partitions and works on several at once, one per core.
Here Spark runs in local mode on one machine with 2 cores. On a cluster the same code spreads over many machines.
PySpark is Spark's Python API, and a DataFrame is a table Spark manages: named columns, their types and rows.
`df.show()` prints up to 20 rows and cuts long text to 20 characters; `df.show(n)` prints the first `n`.
`df.count()` gives back the number of rows as a Python number.
`df.columns` is a list of column names (no parentheses); `df.printSchema()` prints each column's name and type.
